text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- If the minority Social Democratic government gives the nod to joining Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU then it would make it difficult to continue a cooperation with the Centre Party, said Centre Party leader Olof Johansson.

- GE Capital, Sweden's first niche bank with consumer credits as its basic product, is to broaden the financial services it offers with special credit cards, saving products and deposits. It is almost four years since GE Capital took over Finax from Wasa Forsakring.

- Every fourth private post deliverer who received a license in the first quarter is registered at the enforcement service. In total, Sweden has 64 private post companies and the number keeps increasing.

- Industrivarden shares do not deserve their bad reputation for trading at a large investment company discount, chief executive Clas Reuterskiold said in an interview. The discount is not larger than that of the Wallenberg family's key investment vehicle Investor, he said.

- Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, is pushing for Sweden to join Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) at its start on January 1, 1999. The Riksbank published two similar speeches last week, saying that to wait and see how EMU develops before joining will become expensive for the financial sector and for the country.

- Pripps is to set up in Denmark to sell beer to Sweden, according to the head of the new company in Denmark, Bjorn Persson. He said the company could not just sit by and watch as Swedes went to Denmark to buy their beer to avoid the high taxes on beer at home.

- Analysts have lowered their forecasts for tools and speciality steel maker Sandvik's annual profit by seven percent for 1997 and 1998. This means analysts see a pre-tax profit of 4.6 billion crowns this year and 5.3 billion crowns next year. Sandvik has performed below the Stockholm bourse's general index since 1995.

- The Stockholm bourse's only textile company, Boras Wafveri, has the potential to be a good buy but it is hard to value, analysts said. Boras Wafveri moved from the A-list to the OTC-list last week which could threaten belief in the stock.
